papers.title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety lies at the core of developing and deploying large language models (LLMs). However, previous safety benchmarks only concern the safety in one language, e.g. the majority language in the pretraining data such as English. In this work, we build the first multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs, XSafety, in response to the global deployment of LLMs in practice. XSafety covers 14 kinds of commonly used safety issues across 10 languages that span several language families. We utilize XSafety to empirically study the multilingual safety for 4 widely-used LLMs, including both close-API and open-source models. Experimental results show that all LLMs produce significantly more unsafe responses for non-English queries than English ones, indicating the necessity of developing safety alignment for non-English languages. In addition, we propose several simple and effective prompting methods to improve the multilingual safety of ChatGPT by evoking safety knowledge and improving cross-lingual generalization of safety alignment. Our prompting method can significantly reduce the ratio of unsafe responses from 19.1% to 9.7% for non-English queries. We release our data at https://github.com/Jarviswang94/Multilingual_safety_benchmark.

papers.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularity of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, a growing amount of attention is paid to their safety concerns. These models may generate insulting and discriminatory content, reflect incorrect social values, and may be used for malicious purposes such as fraud and dissemination of misleading information. Evaluating and enhancing their safety is particularly essential for the wide application of large language models (LLMs). To further promote the safe deployment of LLMs, we develop a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark. Our benchmark explores the comprehensive safety performance of LLMs from two perspectives: 8 kinds of typical safety scenarios and 6 types of more challenging instruction attacks. Our benchmark is based on a straightforward process in which it provides the test prompts and evaluates the safety of the generated responses from the evaluated model. In evaluation, we utilize the LLM's strong evaluation ability and develop it as a safety evaluator by prompting. On top of this benchmark, we conduct safety assessments and analyze 15 LLMs including the OpenAI GPT series and other well-known Chinese LLMs, where we observe some interesting findings. For example, we find that instruction attacks are more likely to expose safety issues of all LLMs. Moreover, to promote the development and deployment of safe, responsible, and ethical AI, we publicly release SafetyPrompts including 100k augmented prompts and responses by LLMs.

papers.title: Safety at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Model and Agent Safety
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large models, driven by their exceptional abilities in learning and generalization through large-scale pre-training, has reshaped the landscape of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These models are now foundational to a wide range of applications, including conversational AI, recommendation systems, autonomous driving, content generation, medical diagnostics, and scientific discovery. However, their widespread deployment also exposes them to significant safety risks, raising concerns about robustness, reliability, and ethical implications. This survey provides a systematic review of current safety research on large models, covering Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and large-model-powered Agents. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive taxonomy of safety threats to these models, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, energy-latency attacks, data and model extraction attacks, and emerging agent-specific threats. (2) We review defense strategies proposed for each type of attacks if available and summarize the commonly used datasets and benchmarks for safety research. (3) Building on this, we identify and discuss the open challenges in large model safety, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, scalable and effective defense mechanisms, and sustainable data practices. More importantly, we highlight the necessity of collective efforts from the research community and international collaboration. Our work can serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners, fostering the ongoing development of comprehensive defense systems and platforms to safeguard AI models.

papers.title: Enhanced Diagnostic and Interpretable Model for Febrile Diseases Using Explainable AI and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: <p><span>Tropical febrile diseases pose significant public health challenges in tropical regions, particularly in resource-limited settings, where timely and accurate diagnoses are critical for effective disease management. However, existing diagnostic systems are black-box and often lack interpretability, making it difficult for healthcare practitioners to understand and trust machine learning (ML) predictions. Additionally, the existing system excludes younger patients, limiting its applicability. This study aimed to develop an integrated diagnostic system that enhances interpretability by leveraging machine learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), and a large language model (LLM). A dataset comprising 3,914 patient records with 32 symptoms was obtained from a New Frontiers in Research Fund-sponsored project and preprocessed for analysis. Random Forest (RF) was trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation to optimize its performance. The tuned model achieved high diagnostic performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing six febrile diseases. To enhance interpretability, a Model Interpretability Framework (MIF) was incorporated, integrating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for visual insights and ChatGPT for textual explanations. This combination provided users with a clear understanding of the diagnostic process, addressing the limitations of black-box ML models. The system was implemented using Python in a development environment that included Google Colaboratory, Visual Studio Code, Flet, and MySQL for database management. Agile development methodology and Unified Modeling Language tools were employed to create a user-friendly design for clinicians and patients. The diagnostic system was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. The RF model achieved outstanding precision for most diseases, high recall (≥0.97), and an AUC-ROC of 0.99, indicating nearly flawless training performance with few misclassifications. On the test dataset, the model performed better in diagnosing malaria (F1-score = 88%, precision = 85%), urinary tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 80%), and respiratory tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 77%). The evaluated system demonstrated strong predictive performance, correctly identifying 72 out of 99 tested patient cases, with 26 cases misclassified and one case completely missed. It achieved the highest detection rates for Malaria and HIV/AIDS, accurately identifying all cases without false positives. This work enhances diagnostic solutions for tropical healthcare settings by improving explainability and ensuring inclusivity for younger patients, addressing key limitations in existing systems. The integration of ML, XAI, and LLM enhances diagnostic performance and lays the groundwork for future AI-driven healthcare innovations, ultimately improving health outcomes in resource-scarce regions. Healthcare providers should adopt this system to enhance the efficiency of disease diagnosis and extend the system to diagnose additional medical conditions.&nbsp;</span></p>

literature_themes.theme: Safety Assessment and Enhancement of Large Language Models
literature_themes.summary: This cluster of papers focuses on the safety concerns associated with large language models (LLMs) across multiple languages and contexts. It introduces benchmarks for assessing multilingual safety and specifically evaluates safety in Chinese LLMs. The studies highlight that LLMs tend to produce more unsafe content in non-English languages and propose methods to improve safety alignment. Additionally, a comprehensive survey reviews various safety threats and defense strategies related to large models, emphasizing the need for robust safety measures in AI applications.
literature_themes.limitations: The studies primarily focus on specific languages (e.g., English and Chinese) and may not fully address safety issues in other languages or dialects. Furthermore, while benchmarks are proposed, the effectiveness of the suggested prompting methods and safety assessments may vary across different contexts and model architectures. There is also a lack of longitudinal studies to assess the long-term effectiveness of safety enhancements.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster identifies significant gaps in the safety assessment of multilingual LLMs and the need for comprehensive safety benchmarks that encompass diverse languages and cultural contexts. It supports research gap identification by highlighting the necessity for improved safety protocols and evaluation methods that can be generalized across various applications and languages.

literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights the need for further exploration into the adaptability of language models in various recommendation contexts, thereby identifying a research gap in the application of advanced AI techniques to real-world recommendation challenges.

summary: The retrieved literature emphasizes the critical need for safety assessments in large language models (LLMs), particularly in multilingual contexts, revealing that LLMs often produce unsafe content in non-English languages. It identifies gaps in existing safety benchmarks and highlights the necessity for comprehensive evaluation methods. Additionally, the integration of LLMs into few-shot recommender systems shows promise for enhancing performance, although empirical validation remains limited. Overall, the studies underscore the importance of interpretability and safety in AI applications, advocating for further research in these areas.
scholarly_positioning: Existing literature highlights significant safety concerns in large language models (LLMs), particularly in multilingual contexts, yet current safety assessments are limited to specific languages and lack comprehensive benchmarks applicable across diverse cultural settings. While studies have proposed methods to enhance safety, such as prompting techniques, their effectiveness remains unvalidated in varied contexts and model architectures. Furthermore, the integration of LLMs into few-shot recommender systems suggests potential for improved performance, but empirical evidence is scarce. This proposed research aims to bridge these gaps by developing interpretable internal representations that enhance both safety and controllability in LLMs, addressing unresolved tensions in the field regarding the need for robust, generalizable safety measures and the interpretability of AI systems.

research_scope: This study will evaluate the safety and interpretability of multilingual large language models (LLMs) in the context of automated customer support systems. The target population will include users interacting with LLMs across diverse languages, focusing on the effectiveness of a newly developed multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety) over a six-month evaluation period. The intervention will involve implementing enhanced prompting techniques designed to reduce unsafe outputs, compared against a baseline of standard prompting methods. Primary outcomes will include the rate of unsafe responses generated by the models, while secondary outcomes will assess user trust and satisfaction through human evaluations of the LLM's responses. This research aims to provide insights into the generalizability of safety measures across languages and improve the interpretability of LLMs in real-world applications.
concept_definition:
{
  "Large Language Models (LLMs)": "AI models designed to understand and generate human language, specifically evaluated in multilingual contexts.",
  "Interpretability": "The degree to which a model's internal workings can be understood by humans, often assessed through methods like probing or attention visualization.",
  "Internal Representations": "The hidden states or activations within the model that capture information about the input data, accessible for analysis to understand model behavior.",
  "Safety Outcomes": {
    "Unsafe Response Rate": "The frequency of responses generated by the model that are deemed unsafe or inappropriate.",
    "Over-refusal": "Instances where the model excessively declines to provide responses, potentially impacting user experience.",
    "Jailbreak Success": "The ability of users to manipulate the model into generating unsafe outputs despite safety measures.",
    "Harmful Compliance": "The model's tendency to comply with harmful or unsafe user requests.",
    "Refusal Precision/Recall": "Metrics evaluating the accuracy of the model's refusals in relation to actual unsafe requests."
  },
  "User Trust": {
    "Trust Calibration": "The alignment between a user's confidence in the model's responses and the actual reliability of those responses.",
    "Blind Trust": "Trust placed in the model without critical evaluation of its outputs.",
    "Perceived Transparency": "The user's perception of how understandable and clear the model's decision-making processes are.",
    "Appropriate Reliance": "The extent to which users depend on the model's outputs based on their understanding of its capabilities and limitations."
  },
  "Enhanced Prompting Techniques": "Refined methods of interacting with LLMs designed to elicit safer and more reliable responses compared to standard prompting methods.",
  "Multilingual Safety Benchmark (XSafety)": "A newly developed framework for evaluating the safety of LLM outputs across multiple languages, focusing on generalizability and effectiveness of safety measures.",
  "Human Evaluation": "Assessment of model outputs by human judges to gauge user trust and satisfaction, providing qualitative insights into the model's performance."
}
technical_feasibility: The study requires access to open-source LLMs or hidden-state extraction capabilities to analyze internal representations. It also needs labeled datasets for multilingual safety evaluation, multilingual prompt sets for enhanced prompting techniques, and native-speaker validation for accurate assessments across diverse languages. Human participants are necessary for trust calibration and human evaluations, which will require ethics approval. Additionally, GPU resources will be needed for model training and evaluation, along with established annotation protocols for consistent data analysis. If only API models are available, the design should shift towards output-level explanation or black-box evaluation. Missing resources include access to open-source models and native-speaker validation; a feasible adjustment would be to collaborate with institutions that have these resources or to focus on models with accessible APIs while emphasizing output-level analysis.
gap: Prior studies have demonstrated significant safety concerns in multilingual large language models (LLMs) in the context of automated customer support systems; however, they treat the effectiveness of safety enhancements, such as prompting techniques, as fixed, leaving unclear whether these methods generalize across diverse languages and cultural contexts. This matters practically because ensuring safety in LLMs is critical for user trust and satisfaction in real-world applications; therefore, this study investigates the effectiveness of a newly developed multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety) and enhanced prompting techniques in reducing unsafe outputs in multilingual LLMs.
question: How effective are enhanced prompting techniques compared to standard prompting methods in reducing the unsafe response rate of multilingual large language models (LLMs) in automated customer support systems, as evaluated through user trust and satisfaction over a six-month period?
theoretical_mechanism: The independent variable in this research is the enhanced prompting techniques, which are hypothesized to improve the internal representations of multilingual large language models (LLMs). These internal representations serve as a mediator by influencing the model's ability to generate safer outputs through improved safety detection and filtering mechanisms. The dependent variable is the unsafe response rate, which is expected to decrease as a result of the enhanced prompting techniques. User-level outcomes, such as trust and satisfaction, are moderated by perceived transparency, which affects how users interpret the model's outputs. The theoretical framework is grounded in the concept of interpretability in AI, suggesting that clearer internal representations lead to better safety outcomes and user experiences. Assumptions requiring empirical validation include the effectiveness of enhanced prompting across diverse languages and the direct influence of perceived transparency on user trust and satisfaction.
hypothesis: Enhanced prompting techniques will lead to a significant reduction in the unsafe response rate of multilingual large language models (LLMs) compared to standard prompting methods, mediated by improved internal representations that enhance safety detection and filtering mechanisms.

methodology: This study will employ a benchmark evaluation methodology to assess the effectiveness of enhanced prompting techniques on the safety of multilingual large language models (LLMs) in automated customer support systems. Participants will include users interacting with LLMs in English and three other languages (Spanish, Mandarin, and Arabic), ensuring diverse linguistic representation. The intervention will involve implementing enhanced prompting techniques compared to a baseline of standard prompting methods, with safety outcomes measured through the unsafe response rate, over a six-month period. Internal representations will be analyzed using output-level explanations and probing techniques to evaluate their impact on safety detection. User trust will be assessed through calibrated surveys post-intervention, while confounding variables such as user expertise and cultural differences will be controlled through stratified sampling and consistent annotation protocols. The study aims for reproducibility by utilizing open-source models and standardized evaluation metrics across all language contexts.

proposal: This research proposal aims to investigate interpretable internal representations for enhancing safety and controllability in multilingual large language models (LLMs) within automated customer support systems, focusing on English, Spanish, Mandarin, and Arabic. Key concepts such as LLMs, interpretability, internal representations, and safety outcomes will be operationally defined, with safety outcomes measured through the unsafe response rate and user trust assessed via calibrated surveys. The study is motivated by significant safety concerns in LLMs, particularly in multilingual contexts, where existing literature highlights gaps in empirical validation of safety enhancements across diverse languages, particularly regarding the effectiveness of prompting techniques. The research question posits how effective enhanced prompting techniques are in reducing unsafe response rates in LLMs, with a theoretical mechanism suggesting that improved internal representations mediate this relationship, impacting user trust and satisfaction through perceived transparency. The falsifiable hypothesis states that enhanced prompting techniques will significantly reduce unsafe response rates compared to standard methods, with internal representations mediating this effect. Constructs will be operationalized using specific measurement instruments, such as response classification metrics for unsafe outputs and trust calibration surveys for user feedback. The methodology will employ a benchmark evaluation design comparing enhanced prompting techniques against standard methods, with controls for user expertise and cultural differences to ensure validity. The expected contributions include theoretical advancements linking interpretability and safety, the development of the multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety), empirical findings on safety interventions, and practical guidelines for implementing enhanced prompting techniques. Key limitations include potential confounding variables such as cultural differences in interpreting model outputs and the risk of ineffective prompting techniques, which will be mitigated through preliminary studies and native speaker involvement in evaluations.

Major weaknesses: There are gaps in the causal reasoning, particularly in linking internal representations to safety outcomes and user trust. Next band requirements: Strengthening the justification for causal claims and providing empirical support for the proposed mechanisms would improve coherence.

The proposal introduces enhanced prompting techniques and a multilingual safety benchmark, which are valuable contributions. However, the novelty is somewhat diminished by the reliance on existing methods without a clear theoretical framework. Major weaknesses: The proposal does not sufficiently differentiate itself from existing studies or clearly articulate how it advances the field beyond current methodologies. Next band requirements: To achieve a higher score, the proposal should clearly outline the theoretical framework and how it extends existing literature.

The methodology is generally sound, with a clear plan for evaluating the effectiveness of enhanced prompting techniques. However, the proposal lacks detailed plans for controlling confounding variables and ensuring reproducibility. Major weaknesses: Insufficient detail on the statistical analysis and potential biases in user feedback collection. Next band requirements: Incorporating a more robust statistical analysis plan and clearer controls for confounding variables would enhance feasibility.

rubric_scores.level: 9-11: relevant literature used but somewhat surface-level
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal references relevant literature but lacks depth in synthesizing existing work and identifying specific gaps that the research addresses. Major weaknesses: The literature review is somewhat superficial and does not critically engage with competing approaches or unresolved tensions. Next band requirements: A more thorough engagement with the literature, including a critical analysis of competing methodologies, would improve scholarly positioning.

rubric_scores.level: 7-8: approaching PhD-level with some shallow areas
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal demonstrates some theoretical sophistication but lacks depth in discussing the mechanisms and limitations of the proposed methods. Major weaknesses: Limited discussion on the implications of the findings and potential failure cases. Next band requirements: A deeper exploration of theoretical mechanisms and limitations would elevate the academic depth.

The proposal is generally well-structured and clear, but some sections could benefit from improved precision and conciseness. Major weaknesses: Occasional repetition and lack of clarity in terminology. Next band requirements: Enhancing clarity and precision in terminology would improve the overall presentation.

evaluation.comments: Total score: 71.0/100. Academic level: Master's-level. Major strengths: Clear identification of safety concerns in multilingual LLMs.; Introduction of enhanced prompting techniques and a multilingual safety benchmark. Major weaknesses: Insufficient depth in literature engagement and theoretical framing.; Weak justification for causal claims and potential confounding variables. Required improvements for true PhD-level quality: Strengthen theoretical framing and literature engagement.; Provide robust justification for causal claims and methodological rigor.; Discuss limitations and potential failure cases in greater detail. Final verdict: The proposal demonstrates some promising elements but lacks the depth and rigor expected of genuine PhD-level research.
